label: Gastrointestinal
blurb: Acid suppression, antiemetics, IBD biologics, laxatives, liver disease

drugs.name: Omeprazole
drugs.primaryEffect: Profound and prolonged suppression of gastric acid secretion
drugs.treatmentUsage: Gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer disease, Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, stress ulcer prophylaxis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A prodrug activated in the acidic secretory canaliculus that irreversibly binds the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump on parietal cells, blocking the final common step of acid secretion.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 and iron malabsorption, increased Clostridioides difficile and pneumonia risk, acute interstitial nephritis, fracture risk, rebound acid hypersecretion
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent clopidogrel with omeprazole specifically because CYP2C19 inhibition blocks clopidogrel activation; hypersensitivity
drugs.tooltip: Irreversible pump inhibition means acid suppression outlasts the drug's short half-life. Take 30 to 60 minutes before a meal so pumps are active when drug levels peak. Pantoprazole is preferred with clopidogrel.

drugs.name: Famotidine
drugs.primaryEffect: Moderate reduction of gastric acid secretion
drugs.treatmentUsage: Gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer disease, stress ulcer prophylaxis, adjunct in anaphylaxis and mastocytosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively blocks histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells, reducing histamine-stimulated cAMP production and therefore acid secretion.
drugs.sideEffects: Headache, dizziness, confusion in the elderly or in renal impairment, thrombocytopenia, tachyphylaxis with continuous use
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; requires renal dose adjustment
drugs.tooltip: Faster onset than PPIs but weaker and prone to tachyphylaxis within weeks. Famotidine is preferred over cimetidine because cimetidine inhibits CYP450 and causes gynecomastia by blocking androgen receptors.

drugs.name: Sucralfate
drugs.primaryEffect: Forms a physical protective barrier over ulcerated mucosa
drugs.treatmentUsage: Duodenal ulcer healing, stress ulcer prophylaxis, radiation proctitis, oral mucositis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: In acid, the aluminum sucrose sulfate polymerizes into a viscous paste that binds selectively to exposed proteins at ulcer craters, forming a protective coating.
drugs.sideEffects: Constipation, aluminum accumulation in renal failure, impaired absorption of many drugs including fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine, and phenytoin
drugs.contraindications: Severe renal impairment because of aluminum toxicity; requires an acidic environment so it should not be combined with PPIs at the same time
drugs.tooltip: It requires acid to activate, so giving it with a proton pump inhibitor defeats the purpose. Give other medications two hours apart because it binds them in the gut.

drugs.name: Misoprostol
drugs.primaryEffect: Restores mucosal protection and stimulates uterine contraction
drugs.treatmentUsage: Prevention of NSAID-induced gastric ulcers; cervical ripening, labor induction, medical abortion with mifepristone, postpartum hemorrhage
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Agonizes prostaglandin EP receptors to increase gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion and decrease acid production; in the uterus it stimulates myometrial contraction and cervical softening.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea and abdominal cramping, uterine cramping and bleeding, fever and chills with obstetric use
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy when used for gastric protection (boxed warning), prior cesarean delivery with labor induction, inflammatory bowel disease
drugs.tooltip: NSAIDs cause ulcers by blocking protective prostaglandins, and misoprostol replaces them. The uterotonic effect makes it absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy for gastric indications.

drugs.name: Ondansetron
drugs.primaryEffect: Prevents and treats nausea and vomiting
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, postoperative nausea, gastroenteritis, hyperemesis gravidarum
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Blocks 5-HT3 serotonin receptors on vagal afferents in the gut and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, interrupting the serotonin-mediated emetic reflex.
drugs.sideEffects: Headache, constipation, QT prolongation, serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs, elevated transaminases
drugs.contraindications: Congenital long QT syndrome, concurrent apomorphine, known hypersensitivity
drugs.tooltip: The most effective antiemetic for chemotherapy-induced nausea because chemotherapy releases serotonin from gut enterochromaffin cells. Constipation and QT prolongation are the two effects to remember.

drugs.name: Metoclopramide
drugs.primaryEffect: Increases gastric motility and suppresses nausea
drugs.treatmentUsage: Diabetic gastroparesis, refractory nausea and vomiting, migraine-associated nausea, small bowel intubation
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Antagonizes D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone for antiemesis and in the gut, where it also acts as a 5-HT4 agonist to increase acetylcholine release and accelerate gastric emptying.
drugs.sideEffects: Tardive dyskinesia (boxed warning), acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea, drowsiness, diarrhea
drugs.contraindications: Bowel obstruction or perforation, pheochromocytoma, seizure disorder, Parkinson disease, use beyond 12 weeks
drugs.tooltip: The only widely available prokinetic, but the boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia limits therapy to 12 weeks. It is contraindicated in bowel obstruction because increasing motility against a blockage causes perforation.

drugs.name: Prochlorperazine
drugs.primaryEffect: Suppresses nausea and vomiting centrally
drugs.treatmentUsage: Nausea and vomiting from many causes, vertigo, migraine-associated nausea
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Phenothiazine that blocks D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the area postrema with additional antihistamine and anticholinergic activity.
drugs.sideEffects: Sedation, extrapyramidal symptoms including acute dystonia and akathisia, orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome
drugs.contraindications: Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, severe CNS depression, children under two
drugs.tooltip: Acute dystonic reaction in a young patient given prochlorperazine for nausea is a classic emergency department vignette, treated with diphenhydramine or benztropine.

drugs.name: Aprepitant
drugs.primaryEffect: Prevents delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
drugs.treatmentUsage: Prevention of acute and delayed nausea with highly emetogenic chemotherapy, given with a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Blocks neurokinin-1 receptors for substance P in the nucleus tractus solitarius and area postrema, the pathway responsible for the delayed phase of emesis.
drugs.sideEffects: Fatigue, hiccups, elevated transaminases, neutropenia, CYP3A4 interactions reducing oral contraceptive efficacy
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent pimozide, cisapride; caution with warfarin and hormonal contraception
drugs.tooltip: 5-HT3 antagonists handle the acute phase in the first 24 hours; NK1 antagonists handle the delayed phase over days 2 to 5. That division of labor is the tested concept.

drugs.name: Loperamide
drugs.primaryEffect: Slows intestinal transit and reduces stool frequency
drugs.treatmentUsage: Nonspecific and traveler's diarrhea, irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea, high-output ileostomy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Peripherally restricted mu opioid receptor agonist in the myenteric plexus that decreases peristalsis and increases transit time; P-glycoprotein keeps it out of the central nervous system.
drugs.sideEffects: Constipation, abdominal cramping, QT prolongation and torsades at very high abused doses, toxic megacolon in colitis
drugs.contraindications: Bloody diarrhea or high fever suggesting invasive infection, Clostridioides difficile colitis, ulcerative colitis flare, children under two
drugs.tooltip: Avoid in dysentery or C. difficile because slowing transit retains toxin and can precipitate toxic megacolon. At massive abused doses it does reach the heart and causes fatal arrhythmias.

drugs.name: Polyethylene Glycol
drugs.primaryEffect: Draws water into the colon to soften stool
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic constipation, fecal impaction, bowel preparation before colonoscopy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A nonabsorbable, osmotically active polymer that retains water in the intestinal lumen by osmosis without being fermented or altering electrolyte transport.
drugs.sideEffects: Bloating, cramping, nausea; electrolyte disturbance mainly with large bowel prep volumes
drugs.contraindications: Bowel obstruction, perforation, toxic megacolon, ileus
drugs.tooltip: First-line for chronic constipation because it is not fermented by colonic bacteria, so it causes far less gas and bloating than lactulose while being equally effective.

drugs.name: Lactulose
drugs.primaryEffect: Softens stool and traps ammonia in the colon
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hepatic encephalopathy (first-line), chronic constipation
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A nonabsorbable disaccharide fermented by colonic bacteria into short-chain fatty acids, which acidify the lumen and convert absorbable ammonia into non-absorbable ammonium that is excreted.
drugs.sideEffects: Flatulence, bloating, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, dehydration and hypernatremia with excessive dosing
drugs.contraindications: Galactosemia, bowel obstruction; caution in diabetes because it contains galactose and lactose
drugs.tooltip: Titrate to two to three soft stools per day in hepatic encephalopathy. The ammonia trapping mechanism — NH3 becomes NH4+ in an acid colon and cannot be absorbed — is heavily tested.

drugs.name: Mesalamine
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces colonic mucosal inflammation topically
drugs.treatmentUsage: Induction and maintenance of remission in mild to moderate ulcerative colitis; limited role in Crohn colitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Acts topically on colonic epithelium to inhibit cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways, scavenge free radicals, and reduce NF-kB-driven cytokine production.
drugs.sideEffects: Headache, nausea, diarrhea, interstitial nephritis requiring creatinine monitoring, pancreatitis, rare paradoxical colitis exacerbation
drugs.contraindications: Salicylate hypersensitivity, significant renal impairment
drugs.tooltip: Works topically on the mucosa, not systemically, so the delivery formulation determines which bowel segment is treated. Sulfasalazine is the older prodrug whose sulfapyridine moiety causes most side effects.

drugs.name: Infliximab
drugs.primaryEffect: Induces and maintains remission in inflammatory bowel disease
drugs.treatmentUsage: Moderate to severe Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, fistulizing Crohn disease, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Chimeric monoclonal antibody that binds soluble and membrane-bound tumor necrosis factor alpha, neutralizing it and inducing apoptosis of TNF-expressing inflammatory cells.
drugs.sideEffects: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B, invasive fungal infections, infusion reactions, drug-induced lupus, demyelinating disease, hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma
drugs.contraindications: Active infection, untreated latent tuberculosis, moderate to severe heart failure, demyelinating disease
drugs.tooltip: Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before the first dose — TNF is essential for granuloma maintenance, so blocking it reactivates walled-off tuberculosis.

drugs.name: Vedolizumab
drugs.primaryEffect: Gut-selective suppression of intestinal inflammation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Moderate to severe Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Monoclonal antibody against alpha-4 beta-7 integrin, blocking its interaction with MAdCAM-1 on gut endothelium so lymphocytes cannot home specifically to intestinal tissue.
drugs.sideEffects: Nasopharyngitis, headache, arthralgia, infusion reactions, increased gastrointestinal infection risk
drugs.contraindications: Active severe infection; hypersensitivity
drugs.tooltip: Gut selectivity is the whole point: unlike natalizumab, which blocks alpha-4 broadly and risks PML, vedolizumab targets alpha-4 beta-7 and does not affect CNS lymphocyte trafficking.

drugs.name: Ustekinumab
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks Th1 and Th17 inflammatory pathways
drugs.treatmentUsage: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Monoclonal antibody against the shared p40 subunit of interleukin-12 and interleukin-23, blocking differentiation and activation of Th1 and Th17 lymphocytes.
drugs.sideEffects: Nasopharyngitis, headache, injection site reactions, increased infection risk, rare reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy
drugs.contraindications: Active serious infection, untreated latent tuberculosis, hypersensitivity
drugs.tooltip: One antibody blocks two cytokines because IL-12 and IL-23 share the p40 subunit. IL-12 drives Th1 responses and IL-23 sustains Th17 — both central to Crohn disease and psoriasis.

drugs.name: Azathioprine
drugs.primaryEffect: Suppresses lymphocyte proliferation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Maintenance of remission in inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune hepatitis, transplant rejection prophylaxis, lupus nephritis, vasculitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine and then to thioguanine nucleotides that incorporate into DNA and inhibit purine synthesis, preferentially affecting rapidly dividing lymphocytes.
drugs.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, increased lymphoma and nonmelanoma skin cancer risk, nausea, infection
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent allopurinol or febuxostat without major dose reduction, TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency, pregnancy relative, prior azathioprine-induced pancreatitis
drugs.tooltip: Test TPMT and NUDT15 activity before starting, since deficiency causes catastrophic myelosuppression. Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase-mediated degradation, so the dose must be cut by 75 percent.

drugs.name: Ursodeoxycholic Acid
drugs.primaryEffect: Improves bile flow and reduces hepatotoxic bile acid concentration
drugs.treatmentUsage: Primary biliary cholangitis (first-line), intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, cholesterol gallstone dissolution, cystic fibrosis liver disease
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A hydrophilic bile acid that displaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids from the bile acid pool, stimulates biliary bicarbonate secretion, and stabilizes hepatocyte membranes.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, weight gain, pruritus worsening early in therapy
drugs.contraindications: Complete biliary obstruction, calcified or pigment gallstones, acute cholecystitis
drugs.tooltip: First-line for primary biliary cholangitis, where it improves survival and delays transplant. It works by making the bile acid pool less hydrophobic and therefore less toxic to hepatocytes.

drugs.name: Octreotide (Variceal Bleeding)
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage, carcinoid syndrome, high-output fistula, acromegaly
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits release of splanchnic vasodilatory peptides including glucagon and VIP, causing splanchnic vasoconstriction that lowers portal venous inflow and variceal pressure.
drugs.sideEffects: Hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, bradycardia, nausea, gallstones with prolonged use, abdominal cramping
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; caution in diabetes and gallbladder disease
drugs.tooltip: Given immediately in suspected variceal bleeding along with antibiotics and before endoscopy. It reduces portal pressure by cutting splanchnic inflow rather than by acting on the vessel directly.

drugs.name: Propranolol (Portal Hypertension)
drugs.primaryEffect: Lowers portal venous pressure
drugs.treatmentUsage: Primary and secondary prophylaxis of variceal hemorrhage in cirrhosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Beta-1 blockade reduces cardiac output while unopposed alpha-1 activity from beta-2 blockade causes splanchnic vasoconstriction, together reducing portal venous inflow.
drugs.sideEffects: Bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, bronchospasm, worsening outcomes in refractory ascites or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
drugs.contraindications: Asthma, decompensated heart failure, refractory ascites with hypotension, severe bradycardia
drugs.tooltip: Nonselective beta blockade is required because the splanchnic vasoconstriction depends on blocking beta-2 receptors. Cardioselective agents like metoprolol do not work for this indication.

drugs.name: Pancrelipase
drugs.primaryEffect: Restores digestion of fat, protein, and starch
drugs.treatmentUsage: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency from chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic cancer, or pancreatectomy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Supplies exogenous lipase, protease, and amylase in enteric-coated microspheres that dissolve in the duodenum, hydrolyzing dietary fat, protein, and carbohydrate.
drugs.sideEffects: Abdominal pain, nausea, hyperuricemia, fibrosing colonopathy at very high doses in cystic fibrosis, perioral irritation
drugs.contraindications: Known pork protein hypersensitivity; enteric coating is destroyed by acid so a PPI may be needed
drugs.tooltip: Must be taken with every meal and snack. Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K are supplemented alongside because steatorrhea causes their malabsorption.

drugs.name: Orlistat
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks absorption of about 30 percent of dietary fat
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic weight management in obesity, often with dietary modification
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Covalently inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases in the gut lumen, preventing hydrolysis of triglycerides into absorbable free fatty acids.
drugs.sideEffects: Oily stools, fecal urgency and incontinence, flatus with discharge, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, rare severe hepatotoxicity, oxalate nephropathy
drugs.contraindications: Chronic malabsorption syndromes, cholestasis, pregnancy, calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis
drugs.tooltip: The gastrointestinal side effects act as behavioral reinforcement to reduce dietary fat. Supplement fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, dosed at a different time than the drug.

drugs.name: Bismuth Subsalicylate
drugs.primaryEffect: Coats mucosa, reduces diarrhea, and has antimicrobial activity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Traveler's diarrhea prophylaxis and treatment, dyspepsia, quadruple therapy for Helicobacter pylori
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Bismuth binds to and coats ulcerated mucosa and has direct antibacterial activity against Helicobacter pylori, while the salicylate moiety reduces intestinal secretion via prostaglandin inhibition.
drugs.sideEffects: Black tongue and black stools, constipation, tinnitus and salicylate toxicity at high doses, rare bismuth encephalopathy
drugs.contraindications: Aspirin allergy, children and adolescents with viral illness because of Reye syndrome risk, renal impairment, concurrent anticoagulants
drugs.tooltip: Black stools from bismuth sulfide can be mistaken for melena — a classic clinical trap. Contains salicylate, so it carries Reye syndrome risk in children with viral infections.

drugs.name: Alosetron
drugs.primaryEffect: Slows colonic transit and reduces visceral pain
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome in women who have failed conventional therapy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Potently blocks enteric 5-HT3 receptors, reducing colonic motility, increasing fluid absorption, and decreasing visceral afferent pain signaling.
drugs.sideEffects: Constipation, ischemic colitis (boxed warning), severe complications of constipation including obstruction and perforation
drugs.contraindications: Constipation, history of ischemic colitis, Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, diverticulitis, severe hepatic impairment
drugs.tooltip: Withdrawn then reintroduced under a restricted program because of ischemic colitis. It is reserved for women with severe refractory diarrhea-predominant IBS.

drugs.name: Linaclotide
drugs.primaryEffect: Increases intestinal fluid secretion and transit
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic idiopathic constipation, irritable bowel syndrome with constipation
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Agonizes intestinal guanylate cyclase-C receptors, raising intracellular cGMP which activates CFTR to secrete chloride and bicarbonate into the lumen, drawing water with them.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea (dose-limiting), abdominal pain, flatulence, dehydration
drugs.contraindications: Children under six (boxed warning for fatal dehydration), known or suspected bowel obstruction
drugs.tooltip: It mimics the mechanism of heat-stable enterotoxin from enterotoxigenic E. coli, which causes traveler's diarrhea through the same guanylate cyclase-C pathway. Extracellular cGMP also reduces visceral pain.

drugs.name: Cholestyramine
drugs.primaryEffect: Binds bile acids in the intestinal lumen
drugs.treatmentUsage: Bile acid diarrhea, pruritus of cholestasis, hypercholesterolemia, digoxin toxicity, Clostridioides difficile toxin binding
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A nonabsorbed anion exchange resin that binds negatively charged bile acids in the gut, preventing enterohepatic recirculation and increasing their fecal excretion.
drugs.sideEffects: Constipation, bloating, fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, hypertriglyceridemia, impaired absorption of many drugs
drugs.contraindications: Complete biliary obstruction, bowel obstruction, severe hypertriglyceridemia
drugs.tooltip: Give other drugs one hour before or four hours after, because the resin binds warfarin, digoxin, levothyroxine, and thiazides. Relieves cholestatic pruritus by removing bile acids from circulation.

drugs.name: Albumin
drugs.primaryEffect: Expands intravascular volume and supports renal perfusion
drugs.treatmentUsage: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, large-volume paracentesis, hepatorenal syndrome, hypoalbuminemia with volume depletion
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Provides oncotic pressure that retains fluid in the intravascular space, improving effective arterial blood volume and renal perfusion in cirrhotic circulatory dysfunction.
drugs.sideEffects: Volume overload and pulmonary edema, hypersensitivity reactions, hypocalcemia, cost
drugs.contraindications: Decompensated heart failure, severe anemia, pulmonary edema
drugs.tooltip: Albumin given with antibiotics in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality. It is also required after large-volume paracentesis to prevent circulatory dysfunction.

drugs.name: Midodrine
drugs.primaryEffect: Raises blood pressure through peripheral vasoconstriction
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hepatorenal syndrome with octreotide and albumin, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, dialysis-associated hypotension
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Prodrug converted to desglymidodrine, a selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that constricts arterioles and veins without central or cardiac beta effects.
drugs.sideEffects: Supine hypertension, piloerection, scalp pruritus, urinary retention, bradycardia from reflex vagal response
drugs.contraindications: Severe organic heart disease, acute kidney injury, urinary retention, pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, supine hypertension
drugs.tooltip: Do not dose within four hours of bedtime because supine hypertension is the main hazard. In hepatorenal syndrome it is combined with octreotide and albumin to reverse splanchnic vasodilation.

drugs.name: N-Acetylcysteine (Hepatic)
drugs.primaryEffect: Prevents hepatic necrosis in acetaminophen overdose
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acetaminophen overdose, acute liver failure of other causes, prevention of contrast nephropathy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Serves as a cysteine precursor to replenish hepatic glutathione, which conjugates and detoxifies the reactive metabolite NAPQI before it binds hepatocyte proteins.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea and vomiting, anaphylactoid reaction with rapid intravenous loading, flushing, rash, bronchospasm
drugs.contraindications: None absolute in acetaminophen overdose; slow the infusion if an anaphylactoid reaction occurs
drugs.tooltip: Most effective within 8 hours of ingestion but still beneficial later. Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for single acute ingestions with a known time. NAPQI is the toxic metabolite it neutralizes.

drugs.name: Rifaximin (Hepatic Encephalopathy)
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria
drugs.treatmentUsage: Prevention of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy, added to lactulose; traveler's diarrhea; IBS with diarrhea
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase within the gut lumen without systemic absorption, decreasing the population of urease-producing bacteria that generate ammonia.
drugs.sideEffects: Flatulence, nausea, peripheral edema, dizziness; minimal systemic toxicity
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to rifamycins
drugs.tooltip: Added to lactulose after a second episode of encephalopathy, where it significantly reduces recurrence and hospitalization. Its near-zero absorption means very few systemic effects.

drugs.name: Dicyclomine
drugs.primaryEffect: Relieves intestinal smooth muscle spasm and cramping
drugs.treatmentUsage: Irritable bowel syndrome with cramping pain, functional bowel disorders
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Antagonizes muscarinic receptors on intestinal smooth muscle and has direct smooth muscle relaxant activity, reducing spasm and motility.
drugs.sideEffects: Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, tachycardia, confusion in the elderly
drugs.contraindications: Narrow-angle glaucoma, bladder outlet obstruction, myasthenia gravis, paralytic ileus, reflux esophagitis, breastfeeding
drugs.tooltip: Best used as needed before meals for cramping. The full anticholinergic side effect burden makes it a poor choice in older adults, where it appears on the Beers list.

drugs.name: Budesonide (Oral)
drugs.primaryEffect: Local intestinal anti-inflammatory effect with low systemic exposure
drugs.treatmentUsage: Mild to moderate ileal and right colonic Crohn disease, microscopic colitis, autoimmune hepatitis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A potent glucocorticoid with roughly 90 percent first-pass hepatic metabolism, so it acts on the intestinal mucosa while producing far less systemic steroid exposure.
drugs.sideEffects: Fewer systemic steroid effects than prednisone, but still adrenal suppression, hyperglycemia, and mood changes at higher doses
drugs.contraindications: Systemic fungal infection, concurrent strong CYP3A4 inhibitors which raise systemic levels, cirrhosis where first-pass metabolism fails
drugs.tooltip: The high first-pass metabolism is the whole design. In cirrhosis that metabolism fails and systemic exposure rises, which is why it is avoided in advanced liver disease.

drugs.name: Vonoprazan
drugs.primaryEffect: Rapid and sustained gastric acid suppression
drugs.treatmentUsage: Erosive esophagitis, Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens, peptic ulcer disease
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively and reversibly binds the potassium-binding site of the H+/K+ ATPase, inhibiting the proton pump without requiring acid activation or active pumps.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea, headache, elevated gastrin, nasopharyngitis; long-term profile still being characterized
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent rilpivirine; hypersensitivity
drugs.tooltip: Unlike PPIs it does not need an acidic environment or actively secreting pumps, so it works from the first dose and can be taken without regard to meals.

drugs.name: Diphenoxylate / Atropine
drugs.primaryEffect: Slows intestinal motility to reduce diarrhea
drugs.treatmentUsage: Adjunctive treatment of nonspecific diarrhea
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Diphenoxylate is an opioid agonist acting on intestinal mu receptors to slow peristalsis; subtherapeutic atropine is added purely to deter abuse by causing anticholinergic effects at high doses.
drugs.sideEffects: Anticholinergic effects, drowsiness, dizziness, atropine toxicity in overdose, toxic megacolon in colitis, respiratory depression in children
drugs.contraindications: Children under six, obstructive jaundice, bloody diarrhea or suspected invasive infection, Clostridioides difficile colitis
drugs.tooltip: The atropine is a deliberate abuse deterrent, not a therapeutic ingredient. Unlike loperamide, diphenoxylate can cross into the CNS at high doses and cause opioid effects.

drugs.name: Clarithromycin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bacteriostatic inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Helicobacter pylori eradication in triple therapy, community-acquired pneumonia, Mycobacterium avium complex
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking translocation of the peptidyl-tRNA and halting protein elongation.
drugs.sideEffects: Metallic taste, gastrointestinal upset, QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, potent CYP3A4 inhibition with many interactions
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent statins metabolized by CYP3A4, ergots, colchicine in renal impairment; known long QT syndrome; pregnancy
drugs.tooltip: The classic triple therapy is clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and a PPI. Rising clarithromycin resistance has shifted many guidelines toward bismuth quadruple therapy as first-line.

drugs.name: Obeticholic Acid
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces bile acid synthesis and cholestatic injury
drugs.treatmentUsage: Primary biliary cholangitis in patients with inadequate response to ursodiol
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Potent agonist of the farnesoid X receptor, which suppresses hepatic bile acid synthesis through CYP7A1 downregulation and promotes bile acid efflux from hepatocytes.
drugs.sideEffects: Severe pruritus (dose-limiting), fatigue, elevated LDL cholesterol, hepatic decompensation in advanced cirrhosis
drugs.contraindications: Decompensated cirrhosis, complete biliary obstruction, prior hepatic decompensation
drugs.tooltip: Second-line after ursodiol in primary biliary cholangitis. Pruritus is common and dose-limiting, and dosing errors in cirrhotic patients caused fatal decompensation, prompting a boxed warning.

drugs.name: Prucalopride
drugs.primaryEffect: Accelerates colonic transit
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic idiopathic constipation refractory to laxatives
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Highly selective 5-HT4 receptor agonist that enhances acetylcholine release from enteric neurons, stimulating high-amplitude propagating colonic contractions.
drugs.sideEffects: Headache, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dizziness; no significant cardiac risk unlike older agents
drugs.contraindications: Intestinal obstruction or perforation, severe inflammatory bowel disease, toxic megacolon
drugs.tooltip: Its high 5-HT4 selectivity avoids the hERG channel effects that caused cisapride to be withdrawn for fatal arrhythmias. Useful when osmotic laxatives alone fail.
